name: Musicfetch
type: Metadata-resolver -- commercial aggregation API unifying music links/metadata across 40+ streaming and content services in a single call; not an audio identifier/fingerprinter (input is a source URL, ISRC, UPC, or text query, not raw audio) and not a classifier
maintainer: Musicfetch (commercial SaaS vendor, musicfetch.io); paid subscription product aimed at developers, labels, and artists
method: Metadata aggregation/search across partner services -- four documented endpoints: text search (title/artist/album), URL lookup (resolve one platform's track/album URL to matches on other platforms), ISRC lookup, and UPC lookup; internally Musicfetch queries and normalizes data from 40+ integrated services (Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Deezer, Amazon Music, Tidal, SoundCloud, NetEase, QQ Music, JioSaavn, Genius, Discogs, MusicBrainz, Shazam, and others) and returns a unified response, rather than performing its own audio fingerprinting or ML classification
required_input: A source platform URL, an ISRC code, a UPC code, or a free-text title/artist/album query -- no raw audio required
minimum_clip_length: 0 seconds -- pure metadata lookup, no audio needed
classification_or_hitrate: No independently published hit-rate/accuracy benchmark; vendor markets 'extensive and accurate' metadata across '30+ platforms' and 40+ service integrations, but this is a claim about downstream service breadth rather than a measured match-accuracy percentage. [uncertain]
pitch_speed_cover_robustness: Not applicable in the audio-fingerprinting sense (input is a URL/ISRC/UPC/text, not audio); as an aggregator it inherits whatever version-disambiguation each underlying platform's own catalog provides, surfacing multiple official versions/remixes linked via ISRC/UPC, but it has no way to recognize an unofficial nightcore/sped-up/pitch-shifted fan reupload since those are not catalogued releases on the source platforms. [uncertain]
catalog_language_bias: Explicitly integrates NetEase and QQ Music (dedicated 'NetEase API alternative' and 'QQ Music API alternative' landing pages exist on musicfetch.io), suggesting deliberate C-pop/Asian-market coverage alongside the usual Western DSPs (Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music, Tidal) and other regional services (Anghami for MENA, JioSaavn/Gaana for India, Boomplay for Africa, KKBOX for Taiwan/Asia, AWA/Line Music for Japan); no formal per-region coverage percentage is published. [uncertain]
evaluation_dataset: No public benchmark dataset; coverage claims are self-reported vendor marketing copy rather than measured against AudioSet/GTZAN/MUSAN/MagnaTagATune/MAEB-style evaluation
confidence_calibration: Publicly reviewed documentation did not surface an explicit numeric match-confidence/relevance score field in the response schema; ISRC/UPC lookups are exact-key matches (inherently high-confidence when a hit occurs), while free-text search presumably returns a ranked/best-effort match without a documented score. [uncertain]
api_availability: Paid-only, keyed via an `x-token` header issued from the account dashboard (up to 5 tokens per account); no perpetual free production tier -- only a 7-day free trial capped at 5,000 requests that requires payment card details upfront and auto-bills after the trial. Paid plans confirmed live on musicfetch.io (2026-09-10): Starter $50/month for 50,000 requests, 6 req/min, $10 per additional 10k; Business $100/month for 150,000 requests, 20 req/min, $20 per additional 25k; Enterprise $200/month for 500,000 requests, 40 req/min, $50 per additional 100k plus TikTok links and priority engineering support
chrome_extension_usability: CORS is dynamically permissive -- a direct live request to api.musicfetch.io with an Origin header reflected back `access-control-allow-origin: <that origin>` in testing (2026-09-10), meaning it is technically callable straight from a content-script/page context without an extension host_permissions workaround; however doing so client-side would ship the paid, metered `x-token` credential inside the extension bundle, a serious quota-theft/billing-abuse risk given the $50-200+/month metered plans, so a backend proxy holding the token server-side is strongly advisable despite CORS technically allowing direct calls
audio_access_requirement: None -- pure metadata/text API; works without any audio capture, including on DRM-protected or age-restricted video pages, as long as a title/artist string, or a resolvable source URL/ISRC/UPC, is available
client_vs_server: Technically callable client-side given the open CORS policy, but the exposed metered `x-token` (billed per request, no generous free ceiling) makes a server-side proxy the practically necessary architecture to avoid an attacker draining a paid quota; only the derived title/artist text or platform URL would need to leave the user's machine if proxied
bundle_weight_cold_start: Zero bundle weight -- no model/library shipped, pure HTTP/JSON fetch; per-request latency was not independently benchmarked at depth in this research, but as an aggregator that queries 40+ upstream services it plausibly carries higher tail latency than a single-source lookup like LRCLIB or Discogs. [uncertain]
breakage_risk: Commercial vendor with an actively maintained public docs site and dashboard; because it aggregates many upstream services, it inherits the breakage risk of each individual integration (e.g. if NetEase or QQ Music change their own unofficial/internal endpoints, Musicfetch's own integration work is what insulates the end developer from that churn) -- net effect is lower breakage risk for the end user than maintaining 40 separate unofficial scrapers directly, at the cost of vendor lock-in and being unable to self-patch if Musicfetch itself is slow to fix an upstream break. [uncertain] on Musicfetch's own historical uptime/incident track record; no public status-page data was reviewed
realtime_capability: No independently measured end-to-end latency figures were found; low per-minute rate limits on lower tiers (6 req/min on Starter) constrain real-time, high-concurrency in-browser use unless a higher/custom tier is purchased. [uncertain]
identification_fields: Aggregated fields across integrated services typically include title, artist, album, release date, genre, cover art, and deep links to each of the 40+ supported platforms; ISRC and UPC function as both input keys and implicitly as returned identifiers for cross-service joining, since they are also accepted as lookup parameters. The exact full response schema (e.g. whether a numeric confidence score is included, whether ISRC is always echoed back for text-search results, or whether lyrics text is embedded) was not fully enumerable from the publicly reviewed documentation. [uncertain]
isrc_availability: Yes as an input/join key -- ISRC lookup is one of the four core documented endpoints, and Musicfetch explicitly positions ISRC/UPC as its cross-platform matching keys; it is less clear whether every response always echoes back a normalized ISRC field for tracks originally found via text search rather than ISRC lookup. [uncertain]
karaoke_specific_outputs: No evidence of BPM, musical key, vocal/instrumental activity, or word-level lyric timing in the aggregator response; Genius is listed among the 40+ integrated services, but this appears to provide a deep link to the Genius page rather than embedded full/synced lyric text -- no dedicated lyrics-with-timing endpoint was found in the documentation reviewed. [uncertain]
tos_restrictions: Commercial ToS govern paid API use; per-plan monthly request caps and per-minute rate limits are contractually enforced with explicit overage pricing, and the trial requires payment card details upfront with automatic conversion to a paid plan unless cancelled -- explicit reselling/redistribution restrictions on the aggregated metadata itself were not located in the documentation reviewed. [uncertain]
risk_tolerance_note: As an official, paid, ToS-governed commercial aggregator (not a reverse-engineered scraping surface), Musicfetch carries low direct legal risk to the integrating developer; the practical risk is entirely commercial/financial (client-exposed token abuse against a metered paid plan) rather than legal/ToS exposure
cascade_position: Best suited as a consolidated enrichment/fallback layer once a candidate title/artist (or a resolvable platform URL/ISRC) is already available -- valuable specifically for reducing integration surface area (one paid API instead of 40 separate unofficial scrapers), but its per-request cost and low rate limits on entry-tier plans argue against using it as an always-on first gate for every video played
failure_mode: Presumably fails with an empty/no-match response for unresolvable queries rather than hallucinating, being a real aggregation of real catalog services, but no explicit product documentation on error/no-match response shape was reviewed to confirm this behavior. [uncertain]
cost_model_at_scale: Metered and relatively expensive at consumer-extension scale: the cheapest plan is $50/month for 50,000 requests (roughly $0.001/request within-plan, $10/10k overage) with only 6 requests/minute -- a free browser extension issuing one lookup per user session would burn through 50,000 requests quickly at any meaningful user base and requires committing to a recurring paid subscription from day one, since there is no perpetual free tier, only a time/request-capped trial
geo_region_availability: No explicit geo-gating of the Musicfetch API itself was found, but its own upstream integrated services (NetEase, QQ Music, Anghami, JioSaavn, etc.) carry their own regional licensing/availability constraints that would presumably propagate through to Musicfetch's aggregated results for those specific services. [uncertain]
